7.2.m: Vyāsa said: / In the beginning of creation, Mahāviṣṇu, desiring to emit the entire universe, / became Himself of threefold form: creator, protector, and destroyer.
For the purpose of creating this universe, from His right side the supreme person / produced Himself by Himself, named Brahmā.
Then, for the purpose of preserving the universe, the Lord of the universe, / O sage, emitted Viṣṇu, Keśava, His own portion, from His left side.
Then, for the purpose of destroying the universe, O sage, the Lord whose abode is the lotus / emitted imperishable Rudra from the middle of His body.
Composed of the three qualities—rajas, sattva, and tamas— / some speak of the Person as Brahmā, some as Viṣṇu, and some as Śaṅkara.
One Viṣṇu, having become threefold, creates, consumes, and protects; / therefore, no distinction should be made [among them] by the best of men in the three worlds.
The primordial Nature (prakṛti) of this supreme Self, Mahāviṣṇu, / is the primary cause of the existing universe; she is sung of as knowledge and ignorance.
She whose nature is existence and non-existence, the eternal cause of the universe, / suddenly became threefold: Brāhmī, Lakṣmī, and Ambikā.
Having appointed that primordial [female] in creation, preservation, and destruction, / the primordial Person then vanished right there, O sage.
By Her command, Brahmā then indeed created the great elements— / earth, space, wind, water, and fire, the five [elements]—through meditative concentration.
The lotus-seated [Brahmā] created Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and likewise Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, / Tapas, and Satya, and so forth.
Brahmā created Atala, and beneath it Vitala, O twice-born one, / beneath that Sutala, and beneath that Talātala,
Mahātala beneath it, and beneath that Rasātala, / and beneath that Pātāla: the worlds in this order.
For the dwelling of the deities, he created in the middle of the earth the great mountain / with jewel-peaks, blazing like gold,
and Mandara, Carama, Trikūṭa, and the eastern mountain of sunrise, / and he created various other mountains as well.
Then the Lokāloka [mountain], and within it the seven oceans / and the seven continents, O lord of Brahmins, [were created] by the self-born supreme Lord.
Jambudvīpa, O best of the twice-born, and the continent named Plakṣa, / which is to be understood as twice that size, and Śālmala twice that again;
and those continents beginning with Plakṣa are endowed with every region, / possessed of all good qualities, the forms of gods and divine seers.
These seven continents, O Brahmin, are encircled by seven oceans; / I shall speak of the names of those oceans; hear them:
Salt, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and ending with fresh water: / these are the oceans, O divine sage, each subsequent one being twice the size of the former,
all the way up to the Lokāloka mountain, as should be understood. / In each continent Brahmā then [created] trees, shrubs, creepers, and the like,
and created creatures born from animal wombs, O best of the twice-born. / Then the gods, humans, serpents, and likewise the Vidyādharas,
and in succession he created his sons, the sages beginning with Dakṣa; / Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other low-born folk as well;
and that Lord of creatures created their livelihoods and the like. / What is south of the Golden Mountain and north of the Vindhya mountain,
that, they say, is the region of Bhārata, which bestows the fruits of good and evil deeds. / Those best of men who, having attained birth in the region of Bhārata,
perform righteous deeds, are all equal to Keśava. / An action performed in the land of action, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
its fruit the people experience in the lands of enjoyment, O best of men. / He who, having arrived in the land of action, is intent on righteous deeds,
no one at all equal to him is found in the three worlds. / His birth is fruitful, and his life is well lived,
whose mind is not lacking in service to glorious Nārāyaṇa. / Through merits accumulated over ten million births, very firm devotion arises in men
toward Nārāyaṇa, the god of gods, the sole supreme sovereign of the cycle of existence. / [Such a man] bestows all happiness, is worthy of praise, and is fearless.
That country where a Vaiṣṇava does not dwell should be abandoned at once. / Sin accumulated in other lives, whether little or much,
reaches destruction that very instant from the sight of a devotee of the Lord. / But he who carries on his own head with devotion the water from a Vaiṣṇava's feet,
which removes all sins—what need has he of bathing in the Gaṅgā? / He who keeps company with the devotees of the Lord even for a moment
is freed from all sins, even those beginning with the murder of a Brahmin. / Whatever righteous deeds are performed, O lord of Brahmins,
in the presence of a devotee of the Lord, they become imperishable. / Where Vaiṣṇavas stay for a moment, or half a moment,
truly, truly, and again truly, that is a sacred ford, that is an ascetic grove. / Food or water or fruit [given] to a Vaiṣṇava,
whatever little is given, O Brahmin, that gift becomes imperishable. / A Vaiṣṇava is proclaimed to be the embodiment of all deities;
if he is pleased by someone, all the deities are pleased. / In this terrible cycle of existence filled with diverse sorrows,
a man devoted to the Lord never sinks down. / Therefore, you too, O lord of Brahmins, by means of practical yoga,
always worshipping Keśava with devotion, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu! / Sūta said: / Having heard this speech of the great son of the maiden (Vyāsa),
Jaimini, raising folded hands to his head, asked: / Jaimini said: / 'The majesty of the Lord's devotee has been told by you again and again;
O guru, what are their characteristics? Tell all of that now! / Or how are Vaiṣṇavas to be recognized by people, O best of sages?'

Tell all of that from the beginning, if you have grace toward me."
Vyāsa said:
"Formerly, when Madhu and Kaiṭabha were slain by the Creator himself,

hear what the Lord said when asked; I know it.
At the end of the kalpa, having destroyed the entire universe in the form of Rudra,

the Lord alone slept by means of Yogamāyā.
While that Lord was sleeping, bewildered by Yoganidrā,
the entire earth became flooded by an expanse of water.

Then Brahmā, the creator of the universe, upon his navel-lotus,
meditating on that primal Person, stood with his mind fixed on him.

At that most terrible time, O twice-born, from the ear-wax of Viṣṇu
were born two terrible great asuras named Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

Wandering through the intermediate space, those two exceedingly ferocious Dānavas
saw Brahmā upon the navel-lotus of glorious Viṣṇu.

Then, O twice-born, those two Daityas of great strength and valor,
with eyes reddened by anger, made an effort to kill him.

Then Brahmā, the creator of the universe, thinking in his heart of his own death,
praised the divine Yoganidrā with gentle speech.

Having heard the praise of Brahmā, the supreme lord,
she spoke these words with affection: 'State what is desired by you.'

Brahmā said:
'These two exceedingly fierce Dānavas are determined to kill me.
Quickly bewilder them with your māyā; release Acyuta, the protector.'

Then the divine slumber released that Mahāviṣṇu.
Then, in the intermediate space, full of compassion,

he who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge fought those two Dānavas in hand-to-hand combat.
Having fought a most terrible battle for five thousand years,

no one attained victory, nor did anyone suffer defeat.
Then those two Dānavas there, bewildered by Mahāmāyā,

said to Keśava: 'Choose a boon from us.'
Then, laughing, the lord of gods spoke these words, O twice-born:

'If you two Daityas are pleased, both of you quickly become fit to be slain by me.'
Then those two terrible Dānavas, to the Lord, Janārdana,

great masters of illusion though they were, bewildered by Mahāmāyā, said:
'This very boon is given to you; there is no doubt in this.'

'Kill the two of us where the earth is without water, O Janārdana.'
Then, having brought those two great asuras to his thighs,

they were slain instantly, O twice-born, with the wonderful edge of his discus.
Seeing the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, slain by the bearer of the discus,
Brahmā, freed from fear, praised the god of gods:

Brahmā said:
'Obeisance, obeisance to you, the supreme lord, the destroyer of all distress of those who take refuge!
Obeisance, obeisance to you, whose nature is the three guṇas, to Nārāyaṇa of immeasurable valor!

Men, people who take refuge in the pair of your lotus-feet, never encounter misfortune.
This has been realized by me, O you of endless fame: this great calamity of mine was removed at once.

You are the lord of yoga, you are compassionate, the ruler of the three worlds;
you are the god of gods, the protector of those who seek refuge, the supreme ruler.
You are merciless toward the destruction of hosts of enemies,
since I have been protected and these two asuras have been slain by you.

Although those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, were exceedingly fierce,
nevertheless in my mind I consider them your own people here,
since by granting the boon of the destruction of their own lives,
you, the Lord who bestows all auspiciousness, were pleased.

O bee to the lotus-face of Lakṣmī! O god of gods!
O destroyer of the fear and sorrow of worldly existence!
Protect me, who take refuge in the pair of your lovely lotus-feet, O Lord, with compassion; constant obeisance to you!

Be gracious, O lotus-eyed one! Be gracious, O lord of Kamalā!
Be gracious, O lord of all beings! O sustainer of the universe, obeisance to you!

Obeisance to you, who are pleased with devotees; obeisance to you, the giver of devotion;
obeisance to you, whose form is knowledge; be my refuge, O sinless one!

Obeisance to you, obeisance to you, obeisance to you, repeated obeisance!
Save, save, save, O you who consist of the universe!'

Vyāsa said:
Praised with these and other hymns by Brahmā, the maker of the worlds,
that divine Lord attained the utmost delight.

The holy Lord said:
'By this hymn and by your devotion, I am pleased, O lotus-seated one.
Say what is desired by you; I shall grant it to you on earth.'

Brahmā said:
'If you are pleased, O lord of gods, ocean of compassion, you who consist of the universe,
my boon is that there may be no misfortunes for your devotees.'

The holy Lord said:
'So be it, O best of gods! This boon is granted to you by me:
no misfortune shall ever befall my devotee on the circle of the earth.

I constantly dwell in the bodies of Vaiṣṇavas;
therefore, Vaiṣṇava men never incur misfortunes.'

Brahmā said:
'Everything indeed has been granted by you, O Lord of the universe, there is no doubt,
since these two great Daityas have been cast down in battle.

Having approached [you] for however long a time, whoever indeed, O Lord,
praises you with supreme devotion by means of this hymn, you will be his protector.

Ah! You cannot be meditated upon even by the gods through meditations;
that you wander in the bodies of Vaiṣṇavas is a great wonder.

What may not come to be when you are pleased for even a single moment, O Master?
That you wander in the company of Vaiṣṇavas is a great wonder.

Who are the Vaiṣṇavas, O enemy of Kaiṭabha? Or what is their characteristic mark?
How are they all to be known? Tell me that, O Keśava.'

The holy Lord said:
'Even in hundreds of millions of kalpas, I am not able to speak
the marks of Vaiṣṇavas completely; hear in brief, O best [of beings].

The world is dependent on Vaiṣṇavas; the gods are protected by Vaiṣṇavas;
and I am dependent on Vaiṣṇavas; therefore, Vaiṣṇavas are the most excellent.

Leaving aside a Vaiṣṇava person, O Brahmā, even for a single moment,
I do not stay anywhere else; the Vaiṣṇavas are my kinsmen.

Those who are free from lust and anger, who are devoid of violence and deceit,
and free from greed and delusion—those people are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who are without envy, endowed with compassion, desiring the welfare of all beings,
and speaking truthful words—they too are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who teach dharma and likewise observe dharmic conduct,
and who attend upon the guru—they too are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who see you, me, and Maheśvara as equal,
and who perform the worship of a guest—those people are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who are devoted to the knowledge of the Veda and its exposition, always devoted to reverence for brāhmaṇas,
and eunuchs with respect to other men's wives—those people are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who observe the vow of Ekādaśī with a devotional disposition,
and who sing my names—those people are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who build temples to the gods, wear garlands of tulasī,
and wear lotus-seed beads—those people are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those whose bodies, O Brahmā, are marked with my weapons,
the conch, discus, mace, and lotus—those people are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those on whose necks are garlands of dhātrī fruits, O lotus-seated one,
and who worship me with its leaves—those people are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.
Those who apply forehead marks with clay from the root of a tulasī plant / and with paste of tulasī wood are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those who delight in bathing in the Gaṅgā, devoted to the name of the Gaṅgā, / and who recount the glorification of the Gaṅgā, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those in whose house a śālagrāma stone constantly resides, / as well as the Bhāgavata scripture, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those who daily sweep my sacred places, O best of beings, / and offer a lamp right there, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those who make my dilapidated temple new again / and adorn the sanctuary there are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those who grant fearlessness to the frightened, O Four-faced One, / and impart learning to Brahmins, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those whose heads are sprinkled with the water of my feet / and who eat my food offerings are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those who give food and water to those afflicted by hunger and thirst / and render service to yoga are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those who lay out groves, plant sacred fig trees, / and attend upon cows are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those extremely devoted men, O Brahmā, who perform the sacrifice to ancestors / and attend to the wretched, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those who construct ponds and villages, delight in the gift of a maiden [in marriage], / and serve their parents-in-law, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Those who serve an elder sister and an elder brother, / and never revile others, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
In Vaiṣṇavas all virtues exist; not the slightest fault is found. / Therefore, O Four-faced One, you too must now become a Vaiṣṇava.
Constantly worship me through practical yogas, O Lord of Creatures; / everything will be auspicious for you, without a doubt.
Those who view property of a deity, property of a Brahmin, and property of another / like poison, O Four-faced One, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
Free from the devotion of heretics, intent on devotion to Śiva, / and devoted to the vow of the fourteenth day—they are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people.
What is the use of speaking much here, stating it again and again? / Those who perform my worship are indeed to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.
"Let the entire world be created again just as it was before!" / Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord vanished right there.
Then Brahmā created the entire world as before; / and having worshipped Hari with forms of practical yoga, he went to the supreme abode.
Those who read this chapter with devotion before Nārāyaṇa / are freed from all sins and in the end go to the abode of Hari.

7.3.m: Jaimini said: / Tell me the truth of practical yoga, O great-minded Vyāsa; / I desire to learn practical yoga in your presence.
Vyāsa said: / A human body, O twice-born one, is rare on this earth; / having obtained a body, a wise man should practice yoga for the sake of liberation.
Practical yoga and the yoga of meditation are the two yogas proclaimed; / of the two, the first, practical yoga, grants all desires to those who practice it.
The Gaṅgā, the worship of Viṣṇu, and gifts, O best of the twice-born, / and devotion to brāhmaṇas, devotion to the Ekādaśī vow,
and devotion to the dhātrī and tulasī, and likewise the honoring of guests: / these are proclaimed in brief to be the limbs of practical yoga.
Without practical yoga, O twice-born one, perfection is not attained through the yoga of meditation; / one intent upon practical yoga goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Jaimini said: / The limbs of practical yoga which you have declared, O lord, / relate their glorifications, if you have favor toward me.
What are the merits of the Gaṅgā, O brāhmaṇa, and what is the fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu? / What gifts are the best, and what is devotion to the twice-born?
Or what is the fruit of Ekādaśī, and what is devotion to the dhātrī? / What is devotion to the tulasī, and what is the honoring of guests?
Tell all this, O sage; I have a great desire to hear it; / no one else in the three worlds besides you can relate it.
Vyāsa said: / Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born! Surely your mind is pure, / since you have faith and curiosity to hear this secret account.
The virtue of the Bhāgīrathī cannot be described fully; / therefore I will speak in brief; let it be heard with one mind.
One who repeats the two syllables 'Gaṅ-gā', which are exceedingly soft— / I deem that even so his sin departs: it is an elixir for all beings.
The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere, [yet] hard to reach at three places: / at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
All the gods with Indra, having come to delightful Gaṅgādvāra, / perform bathing, gifting, and other rites, O sage.
Those who cast off their bodies there by divine ordinance, O sage— / whether humans, beasts, worms, or others—attain the supreme abode.
In this regard, hear the legendary history being related by me, O brāhmaṇa sage; / by merely hearing it properly, one is freed from all sins.
Formerly there was in this world a king named Manobhadra, born of the lunar dynasty, / mighty and knowing all duties.
He had a sweet-speaking queen named Hemaprabhā, / devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, endowed with all auspicious marks.
Having slain all his enemies in battle, that king of great strength / ruled the entire earth along with its oceans and continents.
Once that ruler of the earth, possessing great renown, / having summoned his ministers, spoke these words with affection in the midst of the assembly:
Manobhadra said: / O ministers, this entire earth has been protected by me; / all enemies have been slain, along with their sons, forces, and mounts.
My own clans have been protected, and the brāhmaṇas have been gratified with gifts; / and all the gods have been honored with sacrifices accompanied by all priestly fees.
My own clans have been maintained with sacrifices complete with priestly gifts; / yet all my strength has indeed been stolen away by great old age.
Being weak, I am not able to perform certain actions; / royal fortune does not shine in a man devoid of capability,
like a woman with aged limbs adorned with all ornaments. / All enemies on the face of the earth fear only so long;
for as long as he has not lost capability, they do not look at him with a pleasant eye, / but when his mind is fixed on that [incapacity], even if he is endowed with all good qualities,
the earth will abandon an old king, just as a kept mistress abandons [an aged lover]. / All virtues are to be obtained by devotion; great fame is to be obtained by virtue;
the highest good is to be obtained by giving; but the earth is to be obtained by strength. / One devoid of capability, a wretch, is determined to be subject to an enemy's command;
that king who accepts the word of fools alone is a joy to his foes. / Therefore, O excellent ministers, having divided the entire kingdom,
I wish to give it to my two sons, if it is approved by you. / The ministers said: / What you have spoken here, O king who knows statecraft,
is indeed our view; there is no doubt about this. / Then, by the king's order, the two most excellent ones came to the assembly:
both sons named Vīrabhadra and Yaśobhadra. / And they were princes endowed with all virtues, speaking pleasantly,
devoted to their father, always peaceful, strong, and dedicated to dharma. / Then that king, the best among knowers of statecraft, in haste
divided the entire kingdom and gave it to both of them with joy. / Meanwhile, a vulture accompanied by his female mate,
having arrived, sat down in the midst of that assembly, O best of the twice-born. / Seeing the two birds who had arrived, exceedingly delighted,
the king said: Why have you two come? Tell me of your auspicious arrival. / The vulture said: I am a vulture, O protector of the earth, and this is my wife, O scorcher of foes.
I have come with joy to see the prosperity of your two sons; / a great misfortune was witnessed for both of them in their previous birth.
We two have come to see their prosperity in this birth. / Hearing this most wonderful speech of that vulture, / the king, his mind filled with astonishment, spoke again, O brāhmaṇa:
The king said: / A most wondrous word, O vulture, has been heard by me from you! / How is the past history of these two known by you?
If you truly know the past history of these two, / then relate it in full, O best of birds, leaving nothing out.
The vulture said: / O king, these two were Śūdras in the age named Dvāpara; / they lived as the sons of Satyaghoṣa, named Gara and Saṅgara.
And at the same time, O king, they died inside their own home; / then, to lead these two away, O king, the servants of Yama with terrible fangs,
with nooses in their hands, arrived by crores and thousands of crores, / and they bound both of those who were insolent with pride with a leather noose,
and brought them to the abode of Death by an extremely impassable road. / Seeing these two, Dharmarāja said to Citragupta:
'Let the whole conduct of these two be investigated, O Citragupta!' / By his command, Citragupta examined from the root
all their deeds, good and bad, and then said to the Ender: / Citragupta said: Truly these two, O mighty-armed one, were high-minded observers of holy vows;
yet there is a certain misdeed found when all their deeds were examined: / having formally set aside a gift, it was not given by them to the twice-born.
By that very deed, O king, these two must go to hell. / A giver who, having dedicated a gift, does not give it to a twice-born,
goes to a terrible hell that causes terror to all creatures. / Indeed, the giver does not remember the gift, and the recipient does not beg.
For both of them, residence is in hell as long as the moon and sun endure; / therefore, these two who stole the property of Brahmins are great sinners, O lord.
Let the servants quickly take [them] to the dreadful hell.
Then, by Yama's command, the messengers, biting their lips in anger, / cast these two into the terrible hell, O lord of the earth.
On that very day, O king, together with this wife, / I was brought to Yama's abode by the messengers of Yama who arrived.
The deed done by me as well—hear that, O king! / I will tell everything from the beginning, causing wonder to the listeners.
Formerly, I was a Brahmin named Sarvaga, born of an eminent family, / residing in the Saurāṣṭra country, and fully versed in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.
This illustrious wife of mine was named Mañjūkaṣā, / devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, born of a pure lineage.
Intoxicated by learning, youth, and wealth, O fortunate one, / as a youth I once felt contempt in my mind toward my parents.
I was praised in many assemblies, living in the forest, performing all rituals, / wealthy, handsome, wise, and devoted to supporting my kinsmen.
Yet the parents of such a man as me were intent on sin, / harsh-tongued, devoid of compassion, and eager for the company of heretics.
Manliness, life, wealth, family, / learning, fame, and all possessions were rendered fruitless by my parents.
Pondering this again and again in my mind, O king, / out of contempt I abandoned service to my parents, which brings auspiciousness.
Because of that deed, O king, along with my wife, by Yama's order, / I was cast into hell by the messengers where those two foremost of sinners were.
Along with those two sinners, together with my wife, O king, / I remained in the terrible hell; hear the length of that time!
For tens of millions of thousands of cosmic ages and hundreds of tens of millions of cosmic ages, / the great torment of hell was experienced, O best of kings.
Then, at the end of hell, together with my beloved wife, O lord of the earth, / I was born in the race of vulture birds, feeding on dead flesh.
And these two also, O king, wishing to reach the end of hell, / were born in the lineage of locusts to experience the fruit of their own karma.
The deed that was done by these two in their birth as locusts, O king— / hear that, I will tell it, which brings wonder to the listeners.
Once a very great wind arose, O ruler of the earth; / flying up, they were cast down by it into the pure depth of the Gaṅgā.
Having fallen into the water of the Gaṅgā, these two delicate-limbed ones / instantly met death, which destroys all impurities.
Then, to carry them away, messengers with lovely eyes arrived, / and celestial aerial cars equipped with all enjoyments arrived.
Liberated from all sins, adorned with garlands of tulasī, / they mounted a divine celestial car and went to the city of Viṣṇu.
They remained there, O king, for the lifespan of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest; / by Brahmā's command they then came to Indra's city.
Having enjoyed happiness there that is hard even for the gods to attain, / they remained for that long, O king, in order to enjoy the difficult earth.
These two of great renown were born in your pure lineage. / For one who casts off the body in the Gaṅgā, rebirth does not occur again.
Even so, to enjoy the earth, these two most meritorious ones were born; / having enjoyed the entire earth for a long time, accompanied by sons and grandsons,
Attaining death in the Gaṅgā, which is difficult even for yogins to attain, / these two will go to intimate union with Nārāyaṇa, O king.
All this former history of these two has been related by me, / by the power of recollecting past births, O crest-jewel among kings.
Having met death in the Gaṅgā, these two have reached this state; / but who will deliver the two of us, wicked souls that we are?
Disrespect toward friends brings the torment of hell to men; / that was seen by me alone, O protector of the earth.
Lack of devotion to parents, O best of the twice-born, causes suffering here and in the hereafter— / in this world it leads to loss of fortune, and in the next world to hell.
I consider the sin of killing a Brahmin and the like to be better, O ruler of the earth; / for from that there may sometimes be expiation, but this one is everlasting.
The tree of merit acquired with hardship, the destroyer of all distress, / men on earth fell with the axe of contempt for parents.
Whatever little is placed in a parent's mouth, O king, scorcher of foes, / Viṣṇu himself eats that, because Hari has the form of parents.
Those who serve their parents—visible deities—day and night, / shall attain all perfection through the grace of the Lord of the Universe.
Those men who remain devoid of devotion to parents for even a single day / remain in hell for that many thousands of kalpas.
Therefore this great suffering has come upon me at present; / when I, along with my wife, will attain liberation, I do not know.
Vyāsa said: / Having heard his speech and comprehended it, O best of the twice-born, / the king became delighted and amazed again and again.
The king said: / A wondrous speech indeed has been heard from your mouth, O vulture! / Yet belief does not arise in my heart or in theirs.
Then a voice arose loudly in the sky, O best of kings: / 'True, true, this is true; there is no doubt about this.'
Then, O brahmin-seer, by virtue of reciting the glorification of the Gaṅgā, / that bird, together with his wife, suddenly returned to his former state.
Kettledrums sounded in the sky; the best of gandharvas sang; / the groups of apsarases danced; indeed, a rain of flowers fell.
A celestial aerial chariot arrived, endowed with every delight; / crowds of messengers arrived, sent by the enemy of Kaiṭabha.
Then that Sarvaga, O brahmin, immediately boarded the aerial chariot / along with his beloved wife, and went to Hari's abode.
Hearing of this wondrous deed, that king, O best of brahmins, / together with his sons and wife, became devoted to the service of the Gaṅgā.
There is indeed no sacred site equal to the Bhāgīrathī in the three worlds, / by merely uttering whose name Sarvaga attained liberation.
The glorification of Gaṅgādvāra has been told to you, O best of brahmins, / destroying all sins. What else do you wish to hear?
Those men who read this chapter with great devotion in a temple, / and those who, devoted to the company of brahmins, listen to it—their sins are instantly destroyed.

7.4.m: Jaimini said: / By your grace, the glorification of Gaṅgādvāra has been heard by me. / Now I wish to hear the glorification of Prayāga.
Let the glorification of the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean also be told, O sage; / no one on earth is able to tell it properly except you.
Vyāsa said: / My child, I am not able to speak fully of the fruit of Prayāga / and of the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. Hear it in brief, O brahmin.
Whatever sacred sites there are in the midst of tens of millions of universes, O sage— / how can they all ever equal Prayāga?
All the gods, headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, / praise the confluence of the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī.
Those who take a bath there in the month of Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn / never have to return from the world of Viṣṇu.
Thousands of tens of millions of cows, sacrifices headed by the horse sacrifice, / gold equal to Mount Meru, and other gifts, O brahmin,
whatever fruit is obtained by the wise in Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, / Prabhāsa, and Gayā by offering oblations and giving gifts to brahmins—
by bathing at Prayāga in Māgha, ten million times that [fruit] arises. / Therefore, of all sacred sites, Prayāga is deemed supreme.
When the sun stands in the constellation of Leo, O best of brahmins, in the Godāvarī, / after performing fierce austerities for a long time by means of bathing, giving, vows, and the like,
whatever imperishable merit is declared by the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, / by bathing at Prayāga in Māgha, that very merit is attained; there is no doubt about this.
Fasting on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in Phālguna / in Vārāṇasī—the fruit which one obtains, hear that from me as I speak:
Freed from the sins accumulated over tens of millions of births, assuming all forms, / raising up tens of millions of ancestors, he rejoices with Śiva.
Even by bathing once in the month of Māgha at Prayāga, a brahmin [attains] / that fruit which comes from worshiping Viṣṇu elsewhere for a hundred tens of millions of kalpas.
By worshiping even for a single day when the sun is in Capricorn— / truly, truly I say—everything becomes imperishable.
For as many days as a man remains there in the month of Māgha, / for so many hundreds of kalpas, O brahmin, does he rejoice with Viṣṇu.
He by whom a bath is taken even once in the waters of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā / is immediately freed from sins, from all major sins, merely by the sight of it.
If people wish to cross the very difficult ocean of saṃsāra, / having bathed in the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, let them behold Mādhava with devotion.
Whatever [desire] men sacrifice their body for there, / O brahmin-seer, they immediately obtain precisely that; there is no doubt.
Here indeed I shall narrate a legendary history; listen, / by hearing which a person is freed from all sins.
There was a very wealthy vaiśya named Praṇidhi / who was solely dedicated to the worship of deities and guests and to devotion to brahmins.
He had a lawful wife named Padmāvatī, devoted to her husband, / fair of limb, endowed with good character, high-born, and pleasant of speech.
Whatever good qualities suitable for women were created by the glorious Creator, / those very qualities resided in her body, O best of brahmins.
Now, that vaiśya Praṇidhi, taking much wealth, / departed for the purpose of trade at an auspicious astrological conjunction on an auspicious lunar day, O brahmin.
From wealth dharma arises; from wealth abundant fame; / from wealth one obtains nobility. What can there be without wealth?
Seeing a person devoid of wealth, even a friend runs away; / an autumn cloud devoid of water—does it not break into tiny fragments?
Relatives exist only as long as food is to be had; / he who has wealth has lineage; he has intelligence; he is a scholar.
A man devoid of wealth is like one dead, even though living. / He whose mind turns away from acquiring dharma, wealth, and learning,
he should be known as completely foolish; the greater the effort, the greater the fruit. / Dharma must constantly be practiced, and wealth must always be earned.
Learning should always be acquired by discerning men. / Through giving, both wealth and learning increase every day;
dharma, however, does not increase [by itself]—it is not preserved without men. / Having obtained wood, grass, or even chaff, one should not discard it.
A man of accumulating habit never perishes. / Then that vaiśya Praṇidhi, having appointed his wife in the home,
skilled in household affairs, departed on his trade. / Now, once, his wife, taking unguents and other things,
went along with her friends to bathe, O brahmin-seer. / Then a man named Dhanurdhvaja, himself an abode of sins,
saw her performing her bath according to her desire— / her who was adorned like a blooming golden flower, her face like a full-blown lotus,
with eyes like a fawn's, lovely, with firm and elevated breasts. / Beholding that vaiśya's wife, that outcaste, afflicted with passion,
laughing, spoke words, heedless of his own form: / Dhanurdhvaja said: / 'Who are you, auspicious one, fair-hipped, sweetly smiling, beautiful?
Suddenly you have stolen my heart with the charms of youth, O dear one! / O slender lady of broad hips, with me, who am possessed of good qualities,
may you, full of good qualities, experience the greatest pleasure!' / Hearing the words of Dhanurdhvaja, her friends then, O brahmin,
spoke in anger, biting their lips: / The friends said: / 'Hey, you fool, wicked one, born of a wicked family!
Even the sight of her feet is not granted to you! / This woman is devoted to her husband, dedicated to righteous deeds.
By those who desire happiness for themselves, another's wife's facial beauty / and another's property are never looked upon with a sinful gaze.
Having looked, fools, tormented by the fire of passion, are burned. / Go far away, evil-minded one! Do not speak such unbearable words!
We would not touch you even with our feet!' / Dhanurdhvaja said: / 'Fie upon this word "caste"! Knowing all good qualities,'

"Now, because I am an outcaste, I was not considered by you.
When gold is filled with liquor, though staying inside a jar,

what man who knows its qualities, having found it, would not take it?
Therefore, make it so that I now obtain this young woman,

O female friends, for I have taken refuge with you!"
To that fool who was speaking thus again and again, O best of the twice-born,

they, seized with extreme curiosity, spoke these words.
The friends said:
"If you surely desire this beautiful woman, O very wicked-minded one,

abandon your body quickly at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā."
Having exchanged glances with one another and laughing, they then, O twice-born,

taking that virtuous wife, went into their own home.
Then that outcaste, out of infatuation, having committed a thousand killings of Brahmins,

desiring her, attained dissolution into the five elements in the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Resembling her husband in form, endowed with all virtues, and mighty,

that very same outcaste arose, remembering his own story.
Then that Vaiśya Praṇidhi, on that very auspicious day,

having engaged in trade, returned towards his own abode.
The outcaste, also, O Brahmin, then entered her dwelling,

resembling Praṇidhi in form, age, and virtues as well.
Seeing those two of identical form standing before her, mines of virtue,

she thought: "Whose beloved am I? Or who is my husband?"
Then that virtuous woman, astonished, seeing those two husbands,
praised the divine Mādhava with words of tender syllables.

Padmāvatī said:
"I bow to Govinda of endless form, whose lotus-feet are worshipped by Śakra and the other gods, / the lord of yoga, known by knowers of yoga, devoid of desire, the granter of yoga, worthy of being worshipped by yogis.
Salutations to you, crusher of Kaiṭabha! Salutations to you, destroyer of Madhu! / Salutations to you, destroyer of the demon Kaṃsa! Salutations to you, feller of Cāṇūra!
Salutations always to the foremost in rescuing the Vedas! Salutations to you, rescuer of the earth! / Salutations to the one capable of bearing the earth! Salutations to you, ender of Daityas!

Salutations to you whose pair of feet is washed by the waters of the Gaṅgā! Salutations to the ender of the race of kings! / Salutations to you, slayer of Rāvaṇa's lineage, and ender of numerous Daityas!

Salutations to you, censurer of sacrifice! Salutations to you, ender of the Mleccha hordes! / Salutations to you seated on the heart's lotus! Salutations to you whose banner bears all enemies [vanquished]!
Be pleased, O lord beloved of the cowherd women, god of gods who held the mountain with a single hand! / Be pleased, O bee to the lotus face of Lakṣmī! Be pleased, O Viṣṇu! Salutations always to you!
Be pleased, O lotus-eyed one, disk-bearer! You are the bearer of the mace Kaumodakī in hand! / Be pleased, O Viṣṇu, holder of the Pāñcajanya! Salutations always to you, holder of the lotus!
In your temple of worldly curiosity, in the darkness of delusion where discrimination is the lamp, / utterly bewildered by your Māyā, O Keśava, I wander constantly.
The lords of the gods, headed by Virañci, Indra, and the Sun, do not know your Māyā, O enemy of the Asuras! / How can I, a mortal woman, know your Māyā? Compassionately remove my delusion before me!"

Vyāsa said:
Hearing her hymn, the Lord Mādhava, the master, / the Lord of the World who grants the fruits of the four aims of life, seeing [her],

suddenly appeared, resplendent like ten million suns.
Looking at the ground, she bowed with her head to his two feet:
"Salutations to you, beloved of Kamalā, giver of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation! / Dispel my mind's delusion, for I am devoid of knowledge."

The Holy Lord said:
"Abandon your delusion, O fair-limbed one, for both of these are indeed your husbands.
With single-minded devotion, O fair-hipped woman, serve them both always.
He who is your husband Praṇidhi, my devotee, youthful and wise, / to enjoy the fruit of happiness, O virtuous woman, he himself became twofold.
Just as Lakṣmī of endless forms sports with me, / so you too, O fair-hipped woman, always enjoy happiness with both of them."

Padmāvatī said:
"O Lord, men do not praise two husbands for one woman.
Deliver me, submerged in the billows of the ocean of shame, O compassionate one!"

The Holy Lord said:
"If you surely fear ill-repute on earth, O virtuous woman, / then come to my city along with both of them, O fair-faced one!"

An aerial chariot arrived immediately by the Lord's command.
Taking those two, she set out to go to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, as she was going along the path with her two husbands, O Jaimini, / she saw a great soul standing on a chariot, accompanied by a woman,
surrounded by a host of four-armed messengers, seated upon Garuḍa, / with eyes like lotus petals, shining like the flax flower.
Then that chaste, excellent woman asked those messengers of Viṣṇu, / who bore the form of Viṣṇu: "Who is this man standing on the chariot?
And who are you great souls, with eyes resembling white lotuses, / all resembling Viṣṇu, with conch, discus, and other [weapons] in hand?"
Then those messengers of the Lord, equal in prowess to Viṣṇu, / having smiled, all spoke repeatedly, filled with supreme joy.

The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"We are the messengers of Viṣṇu, O virtuous woman. Taking this virtuous person, / we are going to his noble abode, the supreme world."

Padmāvatī said:
"By the power of what merit has he reached such a state?
O great-souled messengers of Viṣṇu, ah, tell this to me!"

The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"This Rākṣasa named Bṛhaddhvaja caused grief to the world,
and was a dweller in the forests and wild places, of great strength and prowess.
He took other men's wives and other men's wealth, was ready to harm his enemies, / ate beef, spoke harsh words, and reviled the gods.

Whatever deed was bent on sin, that was constantly done by him.
Not even in a dream was an auspicious deed done by him, O devoted wife.
Having mounted a chariot, constantly tormented by lust, / wandering through the sky to abduct the wives of others, O fair-hipped woman,
whichever woman in the prime of her youth he saw anywhere, / she was embraced by force by him, afflicted with passion, right then and there.
Then once, the beloved of the king named Bhīmakeśa, / beautiful, in early youth, he saw in the midst of her pleasure-grounds.
Then, seeing her radiant like a golden flower, / he spoke these words affectionately: 'Who are you? What are you doing here?'

Then that beloved of King Bhīmakeśa said:
'I am adorned with the name Keśinī, knowing the arts of love.
Ah, me, who know all virtues, who am delighted with love, / born of his own lineage, devoid of fault, the king does not look upon for even a moment!
I must constantly stay right here, whose attention was cut off by my husband, / mourning my own karma, burning with the fire of separation.
Who are you? Why have you come to this garden, O best of beings? / You should please tell me all that.'

Then he spoke these words: 'O full-moon-faced woman,
I am a sorcerer Rākṣasa, and I have come here to embrace you.

Leave your angry husband who always sees faults.
O slender-waisted woman, give yourself to me; I will grant you all supreme pleasure.'
Then, having laughed, this virtuous woman gladly / bound this king of the Rākṣasas with the creepers of her arms, placing her mouth upon his face."
Embracing that young woman distraught with the agitation of discernment, / O fair-hipped one, he mounted the celestial chariot along with her.
Adopting the state of husband and wife, they became filled with great delight; / mounted on the chariot swift as the wind, they traveled on the path of the sky.
Then he said to her: "Look, O slender-waisted one of beautiful face, / having departed from your husband's land, we have arrived at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean."
Then that woman standing on the chariot, above the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, / seeing [it], immediately met her death out of extreme terror.
Having lamented in many ways for the virtuous woman, here also that rākṣasa, / beholding her lifeless, immediately met his death.
"By the command of the one whose banner bears Garuḍa, their sins having melted away, / we are now leading these two of virtuous deeds to Vaikuṇṭha.
In water, on land, or in the air at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, / abandoning their bodies, even sinners attain the supreme destination.
The sacred ford at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean is difficult to attain in the three worlds. / Fasting on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, in Tapas,
even a killer of a brāhmaṇa attains purification there, without a doubt. / Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean and seen Hari, Mādhava,
and having seen the face of Kārtikeya, rebirth does not occur. / Kārtikeya is Hari directly; thus non-difference is always established.
Those who see Kārtikeya all attain liberation. / Listen about the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, a sacred ford superior to all sacred fords.
Dead in water, on land, or in the air, one attains liberation." / Vyāsa said: Having spoken thus, O Jaimini, those messengers of Viṣṇu took them both
and all went swiftly along the sky-path to Viṣṇu's abode. / And that virtuous Padmāvatī, accompanied by both her husbands,
attained conformity with the form of Viṣṇu, who bestows the four aims of life. / Having enjoyed all rare pleasures there, O best of the twice-born,
and having attained supreme knowledge, they achieved conformity with the form of Hari. / The Gaṅgā consists of all sacred fords; Hari consists of all sacred fords;
therefore devotion is enjoined toward both the Gaṅgā and Hari. / Formerly, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, a king named Mādhava,
having performed austerities there for a long time, attained liberation along with his wife.
Jaimini said: / Who is this Mādhava spoken of by you, and what deed did he perform? / How did he perform austerity? Tell me all of that, O most excellent one.
Vyāsa said: / The life of that noble Mādhava, O brāhmaṇa-sage, / listen, I shall proclaim in brief, O you of great wisdom.

7.5.m: Vyāsa said: / There is a city named Tāladhvajā, like [the realm of] the gods, / renowned in all the worlds, crowded with hosts of virtuous people.
There was a king there named Vikrama, born of a pure lineage, / righteous, truthful in speech, and devoted to protecting his subjects.
He had a beloved named Hārāvatī, rare on earth, / who surpassed the brilliance of the moon by the brilliance of her own face.
She alone was dear to the king, even among the group of women, / just as the Gaṅgā alone is [dear] to the lord of rivers, even among the host of streams.
Devoted to brāhmaṇas and gods, after some time, O twice-born, / a son endowed with all auspicious marks was born to her.
According to the rule prescribed in the scriptures, that universal ruler, knowing all the scriptures, / gave him the name Mādhava.
Then that strong Mādhava, O brāhmaṇa, after some time / reached the further shore of the river of all sciences and was endowed with good qualities.
Then that king consecrated his son, who worshipped the host of all gods, / into the status of crown prince and into the kingdom, O brāhmaṇa.
One day, O brāhmaṇa, surrounded by a fourfold army, / he went out of eagerness into the great forest for hunting.
Having slain many beasts there, at the time of noon / he made an endeavor to go from the forest to the city.
While returning joyfully to his own city along with his army, Mādhava / saw a young woman engaged in bathing in a lake.
Her body was revealed by garments suitable for bathing; / she conquered the full moon by the beauty of her own face.
The orbs of her cheeks were radiant with a pair of golden earrings; / her hips were covered by very long tresses, and she smiled charmingly.
Her charming, elevated breasts were like buds of golden lotuses; / her waist was slender like a lion's, and her voice was like a cuckoo in springtime.
That beautiful woman appeared like a banner raised / by the great Kāma in the kingdom of the minds of young men.
Beholding her such, in a secluded forest tract, / what man bearing breath on earth would not fall under the sway of desire?
Then that son of Vikrama, seeing that woman of lovely face, / his heart wounded by the arrows of Kāma, thought:
"None equal to her has been seen on the circle of the earth. / Having embraced her here, my birth would become fruitful.
I am the best among all people in age, splendor, and virtues. / Even if she were Indra's wife, she must still be taken away today.
Whatever fault there is now in abducting another's wife, / who can speak of that, since the king is my father?"
Having thus resolved very firmly in his mind, that lustful man, / stationing his troops far off, went to where she was bathing.
Sovereignty, intoxication, and lust on the surface of the earth— / these three destroy the splendor of discernment; what wonder is there?
His father was a destroyer of sin, a protector of the dharma of men. / Fie! Kāmadeva himself deludes the entire world.
Seeing him arriving with great speed, then / she, alone in the woods, became intensely filled with anxiety.
"Seeing a woman alone in the wilderness, in her youth, / this man runs with speed—so it appears to my mind.
All the sages say, 'Dharma protects when protected,' / but it cannot be known right here what will happen.
Where a place is devoid of help and enemies run ahead, / flight is commendable there; staying brings destruction of life."
Having considered thus, that woman of fair hips then placed the water jar / under her left arm and, out of fear, set her mind on fleeing from the lake.
Then that Mādhava also, O twice-born, with great speed / went before her and stood with outstretched arms.
Glorious Mādhava said: / O beautiful woman, O lovely-bodied one, by the power of my fresh youth / you flee having stolen my heart; I am smitten and senseless.
What is your name, O woman of restless glances and lovely limbs? Who is your husband? / Have you come from heaven? There is no one like you on earth.
O beautiful woman, you are supreme here, endowed with all auspicious marks. / Why do you carry water like a servant-maid, O lotus-faced one?
You constantly carry breasts like golden pitchers on your chest, / and a water pitcher with your hip; O tender-limbed one, this is a wonder!
On the path severely scorched by the rays of the sun, the reddish intervals / between your toes shine like buds of the hibiscus flower.
O fair-hipped one, accept me with affection; set down the pitcher, O fair-faced one! / The end of your misery has arrived merely by the sight of me.
I am the son named Mādhava of the glorious king Vikrama. / With every sentiment, O beautiful one, I shall be a handsome husband to you."

Among the crowd of my women, you shall become the most fortunate,
like the mālati flower among well-blossomed creepers to a bee.

Or perhaps out of pride you wish to transgress my command;
even so, I will not let you go, since I am a king’s son.”

Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words spoken by him, leaving the path, she
stood with her face cast down, O brāhmaṇa, and spoke very softly:

“Even if I would never listen to the words of another man,
yet, casting aside modesty, I shall speak before you.

For I, O great hero, am the beloved wife of the kṣatriya Subāhu;
I am Candrakalā, carrying water for the worship of the gods.
The word that was spoken by you is not worthy of your family: / all those born in your lineage are eunuchs regarding other men's wives.

I am a solitary woman; you are a lord among heroes.
By embracing me by force here, what fame will be yours?

Having embraced another man's wife, there may be pleasure for merely an instant;
what remains here is disgrace, and suffering for more than a hundred kalpas.

This is the land of action, O hero; let merit be performed here.
Do not ever set your heart on abducting another man's wife.

From greed arises lust; from lust arises sin;
from sin arises death, and even after dying there is existence in an insurmountable hell.

All your virtues would be in vain, and your birth also would be fruitless,
if, having fallen under the sway of lust, you should desire to delight with another man’s wife.

My body is fashioned of flesh, urine, feces, and bones;
having beheld only this, have you fallen under the sway of the god of love?

Because of your descent from a line of kings, do you not fear the citizens?
Do you not see the impartial judge [Yama] roaring above your head?

Fish swallow the hook, [for] they are all devoid of knowledge;
if you possess knowledge, why will you swallow the hook when you encounter it?

Discernment in the three worlds is the highest abode of prosperities;
indiscrimination is indeed the highest abode of misfortunes for living beings.”

Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words spoken by her, Mādhava, infatuated by lust,
O Jaimini, bowed down with humility, and spoke these words once more:

“My mind is shattered by the stream of iron arrows that are your glances.
O beloved, save me, save me! I have come to you for refuge.

A woman is dearest only as long as she remains in her youth;
the golden bee does not go to a lotus whose stalks have [merely] buds.

Be gracious, O doe-eyed one! Protect me, your own servant!
Hearing your dry words, my heart is torn apart.”

Candrakalā said:
“Cast aside sorrow, O great hero; hear my auspicious words.
I shall tell what is able to destroy your mental anguish.

On the shore of the ocean, renowned, resembling the city of Purandara [Indra],
in Plakṣadvīpa there is a glowing, famous city known by name.

There dwells a most excellent king named Guṇākara, of great renown,
endowed with all virtues, powerful, equal to fire in majesty.

His wife, named Suśīlā, is endowed with all auspicious marks;
by her service she has won the heart of her husband, and she is compassionate to the people.

His daughter, named Sulocanā, born from her womb, O hero,
surpassed all assemblies of beautiful women by her beauty that matched [her virtues].

Who on earth is capable of describing her beauty and her multitude of virtues?
Beholding that image of beauty, the Creator himself fashioned no other.

O great hero, prince, I was her maidservant;
by destiny I, a fair woman, have come to your land.

There is no fair woman equal to her; there is no handsome man equal to you.
Take her in marriage, if you desire heavenly enjoyment.

Does a strong lion, having abandoned a female jackal even if she comes into his lap,
not hold a female elephant with effort for mating?

An industrious man in this world attains the highest splendor.
Tell me, without effort, what achievement is found on earth?”

Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of hers, Mādhava, the worshiper of Mādhava [Viṣṇu],
dispelling the arising of lust, said to that fair-faced woman:

Mādhava said:
“By what mark shall I recognize that maiden, O lotus-faced one?
Tell that to me, O woman of lovely hips, if you have favor toward me.

Ignorant of the other side of the ocean, how shall I, a mortal, go there?
How will my meeting with her come to pass?”

Of the noble-minded horse named Uccaiḥśravas,
there is a son in your stable, a supreme horse capable of going everywhere.

Having mounted that best of horses, swift as the wind,
you will go to the ocean's shore, whence the earth is easily reached with ease.”

Reflecting upon her words, Mādhava, full of great haste,
his mind troubled with worry, went quickly to the stable.

Having folded his hands in reverence there, the son of Vikrama, endowed with prowess,
spoke thus to the horses endowed with virtues and great strength:

Vyāsa said:
Then all those horses, having heard his words, out of fear
stood looking down at the ground toward one another, not prepared to take him.

Then one horse there, endowed with all auspicious marks,
having stepped before Mādhava, spoke these words:

Whatever grass is left over from being eaten by others is my food;
my binding is with ropes fashioned with millions of knots.

Even in a dream, grains of rice have not been seen by me, though strong, O hero;
what mention can there be of other pleasures here, O prince?

Without honor, O hero, prowess does not belong to the good;
how will fire be born without wood, ghee, and the like?

I am such as this, while all these [others] are furnished with various ornaments;
yet dogs adorned with all ornaments are not equal to lions.

Moving in a clockwise circle over the earth with its mountains, islands, and oceans,
I can encompass it in merely an instant, O king, O lord.”

Torment inflicted by another does not remain forever in an excellent being;
water heated by fire would in an instant become cool.

Sugarcane, through its own sweetness, indeed brings satisfaction even for a moment.”
Having spoken thus and bowed to that horse, the prince,

then at an auspicious moment mounted the back of that steed,
and with a servant named Praceṣṭa, went, leaping across the ocean.

Mādhava, shining, went to the city endowed with all good qualities,
resembling the city of Purandara, brilliant with rows of palaces.

Then, seeing a young perfumer woman present there, the twice-born Mādhava,
with a smile on his face, spoke this very gentle word:

“O elderly mother, I, a traveler, named Mādhava, wealthy,
wish to stay for one day in your dwelling, unknown to anyone.”
That hospitable perfumer-woman then took the guest, / and, rejoicing, went to her own home with great devotion.
O Brahmin, she performed hospitality for him according to the prescribed rule. / Mādhava spent that night with a mind agitated by anxiety.
Then, when the clear morning broke, in the presence of the perfumer-woman, O Brahmin, / Mādhava, the earthly god, related the entire matter.
On that very auspicious day, for lady Sulocanā, / she prepared the rite of fragrant preliminary consecration.
Hearing of the princess's preliminary consecration rite, O Brahmin, / Mādhava became engulfed in a host of billows from the ocean of grief:
"For whose sake dwelling in a kingdom was abandoned by me desiring her, / for whose sake kinsmen were abandoned, and the great ocean crossed,
today indeed, by fate, her preliminary consecration will take place! / Fruitless are all the exertions, however many were undertaken!
Yet people say, 'The foolish man is utterly ruined.' / Let no one's effort be broken once he has resolved on the action."
Reflecting on this again and again in his mind, Mādhava / wrote down the matter described with love upon a garland, flowers, and other things:
"O maiden, I am the prince named Mādhava, son of the ruler of the earth, / the high-souled supreme king Vikrama, who has a palmyra flag.
A servant-maid of yours, named Candrakalā, was there, O maiden; / long ago indeed, the multitude of your virtues was related by her to me.
With my mind attached to your multitude of virtues, having mounted a horse / and crossed the deep ocean, I have arrived at your city.
Now, O fair-eyed maiden, choose me as your groom, / since in this world I have taken refuge with you,
as indeed no other man knows you to be virtuous.
The bee alone knows the virtue of the lotus, not the frog. / Even of the white cloud, there is no arising in the solitary sky;
still, the white water-lily attends on no other than the moon." / Then the hero, the king's son, placed that writing,
along with a golden ring, into the hand of the garland-maker's dear wife with modesty. / Having placed that letter together with the ring inside a flower garland,
that perfumer-woman went swiftly near the princess. / Then, having given the flower garland to that maiden of Balita,
that perfumer-woman withdrew a little distance in fear and stood with folded hands. / Then that daughter of the king, who was extremely learned,
seeing the writing along with the ring, read it entirely from the beginning. / She too, O Brahmin, on the back of that leaf,
the astonished maiden, wrote a fitting answer, all of which is told: / "O prince, O mighty-armed one, all your words have been heard.
Listen, O best of men, to my word, this proper speech: / Today is the preliminary consecration rite; tomorrow is surely my wedding.
No one on earth should abandon an action approved by one's father. / In an enterprise that is difficult to accomplish, however, people should not overexert themselves.
When the deed is accomplished, the exertion is gone; if unaccomplished, the exertion remains. / Nevertheless, listen: I will tell how you may obtain me,
for the sake of which the ocean was crossed by you: / This groom, a Vidyādhara, must be circumambulated by me.
Adorned with various ornaments, I shall step forward before him. / Raising his left arm, let the hero stand facing me;
the one who is able to carry me off shall be my husband. / True, true, this is true; it has been written on this leaf by me.
Otherwise, a firmly settled undertaking cannot be transgressed." / Having written this, that maiden placed it into her hand.
She too, taking that leaf, went into Mādhava's presence. / Reading what had been written by her on the leaf, Mādhava,
O Brahmin, with intense eagerness, wrote a message in return: / "O maiden, O fortunate one born of a noble family, what has been spoken by you,
all that is entirely agreeable to me; there is no doubt about this." / Then, O Brahmin, the perfumer-woman went back near her
and gave that writing with beautiful letters to Sulocanā. / Then, O Brahmin, learning of that writing and the prince's consent,
she became overjoyed and marveled again and again: / "When he has given his consent to that dangerous deed,
is he then Indra himself in human form, or Māyāmādhava? / In this world and in the next, the husband is ever the ground of affection;
even without seeing him, he has been accepted as groom by me!" / Reflecting thus, sighing again and again, that virtuous lady,
on the pretext of bathing, went to the dwelling of the perfumer-woman along with her companions. / Holding that maiden by the hand, the perfumer-woman, a married dame,
showed Mādhava lying on a couch. / Gazing upon him then, who resembled Kandarpadeva,
she saw in succession his whole noble body thrilled with horripilation. / Wherever her pair of eyes plunged upon him,
with fixed gaze, not even a bit would turn elsewhere: / "Is he Kandarpadeva in person, or the son of Devakī,
or Śarva, the lord of the worlds, or Pārvatī's husband in visible form? / In this world, no mortal is born with such beauty!
With him as master, the birth of a fawn-eyed woman bears fruit. / Overcome by my devotion, the Creator with utmost effort,
when I was born as a girl, created him then, did he not? / From this day forward, he is my lord; there is no doubt about this."
Having spoken thus, she resolved to go to her own home. / Gandhinī said: “O maiden, O gentle one, let this expedient be cherished in your heart as well.”
A man does not appear of such fair form even by censure. / Exhilaration, languor of limbs, a tender glance, and astonishment—
all these are marks of Viṣṇu in sleep, O deer-eyed one! / Due to the quiver of his bitten lips, he surely does not wake when spoken to."
Slowly, she showed his hand with her own hands: / "Listen, [Mādhava]: holding herself together, the king's daughter has come to see you!"
Hearing this, he too arose, his mind overcome with flurry. / Bowed down with modesty, Mādhava spoke this word to her.
Mādhava said: "O maiden, my birth has borne fruit, and my exertion is fruitful; / your lovely lotus face has been beheld by me in person!
With all your youthful charms, O maiden, choose me as your groom! / On earth, there is no other groom suitable for you except me, O beautiful one!"
Sulocanā said: "O noble-paced one, you shall be my husband by great good fortune. / The word that was spoken by me is indeed very firm.
Give me leave, O fortunate one; I am going to my own mansion." / Mādhava said: "If I say 'Stay,' O maiden, then pride may arise;
the word 'Go' does not come from my mouth. / Reflecting by yourself, O fair-limbed one, let whatever is proper be done.
Be very devoted to that word in truth." / Addressed thus by him, that maiden, delighted, went to her own house.
Right there Mādhava remained, surrounded by many attendants; / indeed, the charming Vidyādhara groom stood as a Vidyādhara.
And all the people stationed there, adorned with garlands and sandalwood / and wearing divine garments, shone like hosts of gods.
In some places there was singing, in some dancing, in some the sound of tumult; / in some place or other, a row of lamps shone in that city.
With the neighing of herds of horses, and indeed the trumpeting of elephants, / and with the joyful cries of birds, the ten directions were filled.
With various hosts of banners and white royal mansions, / the entire sky all around was indeed covered there, O Jaimini.
Some blew conches, [some] sounded large drums, kettle-drums, and cymbals, / while others played upon the madhukohalaka and other instruments.
Then all the young women, their breasts like lotus buds, / their faces resembling the moon, sang charming, sweet songs.
With garlands fallen from the friction of their youthful bodies rubbing together, / and with fragrances dripping in sweat-water, the ground there shone like a maiden.
Ascending the palanquin made of gāmbhārī wood, / surrounded by her kinsmen, the fair-eyed, beautiful maiden went to the bridegroom's place.
Meanwhile, this son of Vikrama, having fallen asleep upon his bed, / did not realize, through fate, the marriage rites of the fair-eyed maiden Sulocanā.
For those bewildered by the hundred illusions of the Creator, there can never be happiness in this world; / therefore, this man, having forgotten his secret appointment, happily succumbed to sleep.
Abandoning the forest out of fear of fire, the lotus-creeper entered the water for relief, / [yet] is scorched even there by the fire of frost; what is one's destiny cannot be otherwise.

Let people study all the treatises beginning with the Vedas; let them indeed render service to kings; / let them perform fierce asceticism every day—still, fortune does not wait upon one completely devoid of luck.
Sorrows and joys abide upon one's head; / at another time, O best of men, other ones arrive by force.
Seeing that Mādhava had fallen asleep and was destined for grief, / Praceṣṭa, knowing the secret meeting arranged between the two, thought:
“Fie on this prince! Deluded by the illusion of fate, / forgetting his own rendezvous, he has given himself over to sleep.
That maiden, arriving with difficulty, is now near the groom; / what will happen in her eyes if such a rendezvous becomes fruitless?
Stay, you wicked-doer, submitting to sleep upon your head! / Mounting a horse, that excellent woman must be carried off by me.
He joyfully gains a jewel of a girl and a jewel that is difficult to obtain! / Then what is the use of serving this foolish Mādhava?”
Service to kings is performed with wholehearted devotion for the sake of wealth. / If that [wealth] is obtained spontaneously with joy, what is the point of the misery of service?
Reflecting thus, Praceṣṭa mounted the horse / and went through the aerial path to where that princess was staying.
Circumambulating her bridegroom and remembering her own agreement, / she raised her left hand and stood before Vidyādhara.
Grasping that maiden by the hand with great speed, / the mighty Praceṣṭa placed her behind him on that horse.
Taking the princess, he then beheld the exceedingly beautiful city of Kāñcī. / Filled with great haste, Praceṣṭa,
Taking her hand, his mind freed from fear, / Praceṣṭa spoke: “This city named Kāñcī, situated upon the shore within the ocean—
behold it, renowned everywhere, granting all kinds of happiness to people! / Here, whether of the hero Mādhava or of that Vidyādhara—
nor of anyone else, O moon-faced lady! Behold / the series of flames of love's fire clinging to the fuel of my heart!
Grant, O beautiful woman, the accomplished release with the hands of your jar-like breasts! / Upon this lovely lotus of your face, the bee of my face now [settles].”
on this charming lotus-face of yours. What unknowing person holds back here, my beloved? / From the touch of your lovely limbs, the god of love pierces me with his arrows.
Save me, save me, beloved, save me! I have come to you for refuge! / Beholding that fool who was speaking thus, the excellent woman,
Her whole body scorched by the fire of grief, she thought in her mind: / “This fool of evil conduct is named Praceṣṭa by the Creator.
upon my forehead? Alas, through him I am undone! / Where is my mother, where is my father, and where is the bridegroom Vidyādhara?
I have been brought here by him; fie on the arrangement of fate! / In vain do people always indulge in pride in this world.
yet the Creator knows how to cut down the tree of pride with the sword of his decrees. / Even so, in misfortune, patience and utter fearlessness [are necessary],
And the four expedients are commended by far-sighted men.” / Deliberating thus in her heart, the maiden [spoke] with words of tender syllables:
spoke to Praceṣṭa in words of tender syllables. / Sulocanā said: / Make your mind steady, O hero! I am an unmarried maiden;
how will you succumb to delusion by embracing me, O evil-minded one? / Take me, O hero, in marriage according to the rite prescribed by the scriptures;
I will render service to you like a handmaid—of this what doubt is there? / You are my life, my friend, my ornament, and my kinsman.
“Women have no other recourse; do you not understand proper conduct? / Bring the articles suitable for a wedding for the sake of our marriage!”
Take my hand in marriage quickly; take sluggishness to your house! / Her speech was firm on the inside and smooth on the outside, like a jujube fruit;
hearing it, that fool felt the greatest delight. / Setting the horse and that maiden in one place, the evil-minded man
Taking her hand-bracelet, he went to that city; / then she contemplated fate, which is surely most commendable.
since that fool had departed rejoicing, abandoning both of us. / What should be done? Where should I go? Where should I stay now?
In this exceedingly difficult situation, how can my deliverance come about? / If I stay here, what will they say then?
Having reached a holy pilgrimage place, with the desire for another birth, / I will go to dissolution into the five elements, since that too brings the highest good.
Because of separation from me, this fool, and also Vidyādhara and Mādhava— / remembering me, all three of these will not live for even a moment.
While I remain alive, the preservation of their lives may occur; / but if I am dead, these three will surely go to death.
When those men give up their lives on my account here, / I will then certainly share in their slaughter.
Now the blessed lord Hari should be worshipped at holy pilgrimage places; / when he is pleased, everything good will indeed happen to me.
When life is lost, everything is lost; / when life remains, everything is accomplished little by little.

When the night has ended and the cooling moon has been driven far away by the blazing sun, / does not the lotus plant, possessing a mass of fragrant flowers, exceedingly beautiful, attain union with the best of bees?

Having reflected thus in her heart, that excellent woman mounted that exceedingly swift horse / and went to the confluence of the ocean and Viṣṇu's wife to perform austerity, in order to meet the best of the wise.
At that holy, excellent sacred site, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, / there lived a king named Suṣeṇa, born of the lunar lineage.
She thought in her mind of going to the assembly of that king: / 'How can I, a young woman, have an audience with the king?
The threads of the preliminary marriage rite with dūrvā grass are on my arm; / I am an unmarried girl, mounted on a horse, devoid of companions.
My conduct will surely cause wonder in their minds; / having disguised myself, I will go to the assembly of the king.'
By the power of illusion, having assumed the form of a man, / she entered the assembly of the king, like Sudharmā, O Jaimini.
Approaching mounted on a horse with a spear in hand, appearing like an accomplished warrior, / the king himself asked: 'Who are you? From where have you come here?'
Hearing this question of his, that maiden in the form of a man / bowed and spoke to the king, the friend and refuge of the virtuous:
'O King, I am named Vīravara, the son of a lord of the earth; / I have come to your kingdom right now for employment.
Whatever task may be impossible, that alone I accomplish; / as long as I remain, my master will nowhere suffer defeat.'

7.6.m: The king said: / 'Stay right here, O mighty-armed one, in my exceedingly beautiful kingdom! / A livelihood must be provided to you by me; of this there is no doubt.'
Then Vīravara dwelt continually in the presence of that lord of the earth, / O twice-born one, his mind dedicated to his service.
Then once, in his city, O Jaimini, a rhinoceros named Bhīmanāda / continually harassed all the subjects.
Then, for its destruction, the king angrily sent him; / thereupon Vīravara went with the people to slay that rhinoceros.
Holding a spear, he saw that rhinoceros sleeping on the ground, / mountain-like in form, its mouth terrifying with tusks.
Wheeling the horse in the sky, Vīravara, filled with wrath, / spoke thus to that rhinoceros in a voice deep as a thundercloud:
'Whatever trees of sin were cultivated by you, O evil-souled one, / they have all borne fruit, just as trees do when their season arrives.
Whatever living beings in this kingdom were devoured by you, sinner, / you will have an audience with all of them in the abode of Yama!
Cast off your sleep, O wicked one! Behold me, your own bringer of death! / What will you do with this sleep, O great sleeper?'
Then he too rose up, his eyes blood-red with anger, / his whole body gray with dust, having cast off sleep, exceedingly mighty.
Bhīmanāda said: / 'Do not be proud, O foolish-minded one! Your life has come to its end; / merely by seeing me, who indeed is released?'
Just as a moth enters a mass of blazing flames of fire, / even so you will fall into the mass of fire of my wrath.
To look at him who was speaking thus with that sharp spear, / he blazed up with great wrath, making a roaring sound of ‘Huṃ!’
Then that rhinoceros, his life departed, fell upon the surface of the earth, / shaking the whole earth, inundated with a flood of his own roar.
Seeing the rhinoceros fallen on the shore of the ocean and the Gaṅgā, O twice-born, / he proceeded to go near that king.
Going along the road, O brahmin-seer, he saw a noble being, / blazing with splendors like a second sun.
accompanied by the hosts of Viṣṇu's attendants, adorned with a garland of tulasī, / wearing divine garments, celestial, mounted upon a chariot, with a smiling face.
Then, with devotion, he—the best of heroes—inquired of him: / 'Who are you? Whence have you come here? Where are you going? Tell us.'
The man said: “O maiden disguised in male attire, hear my story; / I shall tell it in brief, if you joyfully wish to hear.
Formerly, I was a king, a forest-fire to the family of thieves, / known as Dharmabuddhi, devoted to all duties.
All sacrifices were performed by me, and all kinds of gifts [bestowed]; / and the earth was protected by me for four thousand years.
On the advice of heretics, the land of a twice-born was / confiscated by me in anger; never before had it been found fault with.
Because of that offence committed by me, Fate itself then, / instantly and in anger, stripped away all my royal fortune.
Then, bereft of my wealth, my mind burnt by the fire of grief, / after some days, O virtuous woman, I came under the sway of King Yama.
Seeing me, that deed was disclosed by Citragupta, / and the lord, the sun's son [Yama], whose gait is graceful and who has a lovely smile, was told:
‘This king Dharmabuddhi has always performed virtuous deeds; / yet he has a small transgression. Hear that; I shall speak:
Instructed by heretics, he indeed confiscated the grant to the twice-born; / by that very deed his place is in the hell that is difficult to cross.
By whomsoever the livelihood of another is severed, O son of Sūrya, / he incurs the guilt of his slaying; so it is determined in the scriptures.
Therefore this evil-doer, this king, is a killer of a brāhmaṇa; / his place shall be in hell for hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Whoever takes away land, whether given by himself or given by another, / goes to hell along with a crore of his family line, O Lord.
Whoever steals the land of a deity or of a brāhmaṇa, / no expiation is seen for him for hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Whoever protects the earth given by another, from the one who protects [it], / he obtains merit a crore times greater than the giver's merit.’
Then, by Yama's order, having eaten putrid mud, / injury to living beings in the form of a rhinoceros was committed by me at all times.
Cows and brāhmaṇas, as well as other living beings, / were slain by me, a wicked one, in thousands of crores.
Impelled by time, O virtuous woman, you struck down me, / the resting-place of all destructive acts, born into the womb of a rhinoceros.
The holy bath of the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean is difficult to attain even for deities; / having met death even on dry land there, this good state of mine has come to be.
Go, O fair-hipped maiden! May good fortune be yours, there is no doubt; / in no long time you will have the sight of your husband.'
Vyāsa said: / Having heard these exceedingly wonderful words of his, that maiden / bowed to the feet of him, the king Dharmabuddhi.
Then, ascending the chariot, that king went to heaven; / and that best of heroes too, O brahmin, went to the assembly of the king.
And the king, hearing that the rhinoceros of terrifying prowess was dead, / gave to him in marriage his own maiden, Jayantī.
Taking that Jayantī, that maiden having the form of a man / set her mind to perform austerities at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean at dawn, O best of the twice-born, / she would worship the lord Nārāyaṇa with songs, instruments, and dances.
Taking vegetarian food, sacred sacrificial offering, and fruit, O best of the twice-born, / sometimes that excellent woman also observed a fast.
Seeing her alone, who took her here on the face of the earth? / Thinking, ‘He is a low person,’ she mounted the horse,
and that excellent woman went back again to her own kingdom, / through separation from Mādhava or from that Vidyādhara.
that king's daughter died, since she would not resort to any other. / When she died, that servant departed at his will.
Lamenting greatly there, Praceṣṭa, filled with immense sorrow, / went to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean to die.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, adorned with tulasī and clay, / Praceṣṭa, with folded hands, addressed Bhīṣma's mother:
'In your pure water, O mother, I abandon this body here; / Sulocanā is alone, so may you act in accordance with the truth.'
As he was saying this repeatedly, her attendants, / binding him with a rope, led him to her celebrated assembly.
Aggrieved, by order of the best of heroes, those very fierce attendants / put the completely bewildered Praceṣṭa into prison.
At that very time, seeing that wondrous deed, / a great outcry of lamentation arose in that kingdom, O best of the twice-born.
Having heard of this wondrous deed, that king, a mine of virtues, / arrived, deeply distressed, and spoke, O best of the twice-born:
Quiver-bearers, chariot-warriors, shield-bearers, rhinoceros-riders [or sword-bearers], / bowmen, and spear-bearers, by thousands of crores upon crores—
in every place in that city, the king, overcome with grief, / appointed them then for protection, O best of the twice-born.
Commanded by him, all those warriors of boundless prowess, / swiftly intent on protecting their master, stood in that city in anger.
Songs by all singers, dances by dancers, / and musical instruments by instrumentalists were abandoned there out of fear.
Then that king, O brahmin-seer, summoned his ministers / and, his mind stricken with grief, asked: 'What is this?'
