The ministers said: / 'O lord, this wondrous deed has never been seen nor heard anywhere; / amid so many people watching, where has she gone?
Someone says: 'She was Lakṣmī, who came to earth due to a curse; / just now she has disappeared on her own from your palace.'
'That woman, made of illusion, stayed in your house by illusion; / having shown her own illusion, she has left,' so others say.
Some say: 'That woman endowed with all auspicious marks / will come again, for Indra has the vulva-marks.'
Some say she was taken by the moon to gain high distinction, / thinking her face to be like the moon, reflecting within himself:
Some say: 'That maiden, whose deep longing arose from good qualities, / having a face resembling the full moon, was swallowed by the moon in delusion.'
'Mistaking her for a lotus pool, she was taken by the elephants of the quarters—having a blossoming lotus-face, / lotus-stalk-like arms, and breasts like lotus buds.'
Some say: 'Having created her, wishing to create another woman, O king, / upon seeing that no match for her form could be seen, [the Creator] has taken her who was situated in beauty and virtues.'
Some said, ‘O king, all directions were conquered by you; / she has gone to heaven to conquer the celestial maidens with her beauty.’
Then those ministers, looking at the beauty of one another's faces, / became as if paralyzed, all devoid of energy and full of fear.
The king said, ‘O Sulocanā, daughter, where have you gone, leaving me?’ / Having spoken thus, that ruler of the earth fell unconscious upon the ground.
Seeing the king fallen in immense grief, / an outcry of lamentation arose in that city, O best of the twice-born.
O brahmin, an echo was produced in response to that sound of wailing; / the people there fancied that the ten directions were wailing.
Supporting the king whose limbs were grey with dust and whose hair was disheveled, / all the ministers quickly came to the palace.
Then the Vidyādhara there, the son of the illustrious King Vikrama, / embracing her seat, wept with plaintive cries:
‘Ah, my beloved, whose side-glances are tremulous, with the luster of a golden flower! / Plunging me into the ocean of grief, where have you gone, O fair-faced one?
What fault of mine was seen by you, who are faultless, O beloved? / Why do you not grant me a sight [of you], O auspicious, lotus-faced one?
I shall not live even for a single moment without you, O auspicious woman; / therefore, granting me a sight [of yourself], let the preservation of my life be done!
What use are riches to me, what use are people, what use are friends, or what use are wealthy houses, / if, O auspicious woman, I do not attain you, who are dearer than life itself?’”
Having uttered this and other great laments, O sage among brahmins, / he resolved upon death through grief and went to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Having bathed there in the water of the Gaṅgā mixed with the water of the ocean, / he offered water-oblation to the sun, bowed to Mother Gaṅgā, and said:
“O goddess Gaṅgā, mother of the universe! In your spotless water / I abandon my body, so that you may grant that I obtain her again!”
To him who was speaking thus, O Brahmin, the excellent servants of that [king] then, / enraged, meted out an appropriate treatment for the excellent warrior.
Then Vīravara said: “Who are you, sir? Whence have you come? / Why are you abandoning your body here? Tell that to me!”
Hearing this speech of his, Vidyādhara then / recounted the entire story, which caused amazement to those who heard it.
[Vīravara said:] “Now, you are the foremost among foolish men, without a doubt! / Whether she was a Gandharva, a Rākṣasa woman, a snake-woman, or a Kinnara woman,
that maiden has vanished on her own, as if because her curse came to an end. / That maiden, divine in form, has gone to the abode of the gods.
How will you see her again? / The nectar belonging to the husband of Rohiṇī in the sky is to be drunk by the cakora bird;
can wicked crows, even though strong, obtain it? / What is not to be obtained cannot be obtained, and what is to be obtained is acquired.
No person who knows that falls into delusion. / A maiden is given by someone, and a maiden is taken by someone.
Whatever maiden belonged [to him] in a former life, that maiden the husband obtains. / A wife serves the purpose of having sons; sons serve the purpose of the ancestral cakes.
For this reason alone the wise take a wife. / In accordance with what a woman gives in this world, so does she receive.
Even though crying in the night, the bee must endure the night-lotus; / even a handsome husband does not bring satisfaction to women.
Even while the sun is present, the black bee drinks the nectar of the day-lotus. / An ever-fixed mind upon women, disregard for devotion to Viṣṇu,
and the abandonment of the body because of some sorrows: these three are mockeries for men. / Wives, sons, likewise a brother, lands, and likewise kinsmen—
all these may be obtained again, but the vital breaths cannot be obtained again. / Sensual pleasure was not enjoyed, dharma was not practiced, and ritual action was not performed by you.
When the present [life] is gone, O fool, a future birth will be hard to attain. / ‘My mother, my father, my wife, my brother, my wealth’—
through such possessiveness the life of men goes utterly in vain.” / Having been properly instructed thus by that excellent wise man,
he abandoned his dejection and stayed right there, O Jaimini. / But then Gandhinī, laughing with joy, went to her own house.
And having gone, she saw Mādhava sleeping on the couch. / Gandhinī said: “Arise, arise, you of evil intellect! Your wandering has become fruitless!
At the time of the wedding, that maiden vanished on her own!” / Hearing her words, Mādhava stood up.
Agitated by great griefs, rolling on the ground, he lamented: / “There is no fault in the maiden, nor is there any in Vidyādhara.
All the fault is mine alone, since I shared the company of a vile person. / When association with a base person is formed, fate grants no happiness to a man.
Only this has been understood by me, since this condition has befallen me. / Even a great man attains no happiness through association with a base person.
Through association with ghosts, Mahādeva went naked, with broken ornaments. / Entering an inferior abode, a base person looks upon the wife, wealth, and other belongings.
Having found some slight occasion, he becomes six-mouthed, having six faces. / Hearing of the virtue of the good, a base person immediately becomes despondent.
When he manages to hear of a fault, he assumes a hundred forms at that time. / A wise man desiring his own welfare should never make an agreement with the base.
Even for a single moment a wise man should not make an agreement with the base. / Even for a single step a wise man does not walk with the base.
At a word of trust, a base person immediately becomes disheartened; / when he is able to hear a fault, he eagerly comes to hear it.
Then, having seized the moment, he proclaims it with loud laughter. / One thing in the mind, one in speech, and one in action belongs to the self-controlled;
one thing in the mind, another in speech, and another in action belongs to the wicked. / If that princess had married,
even a slight grief would not have arisen in my heart then. / If that maiden endowed with all auspicious marks had gone to heaven,
she was carried off by a base person—this grief has become unbearable in my heart! / Everywhere I see that fair-faced maiden as if painted;
I cannot forget her while this soul lives. / Fallen into the lap of a base man, that virtuous lady will not live for a moment.
Vidyādhara too will not survive the terrible sorrows because of her. / Just as mother, father, and country were abandoned by me to obtain her,
in the very same way my vital breaths must be abandoned now, there is no doubt about this. / In order to obtain her again, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean
I will abandon my life!” Having made this firm resolve, he set out to go. / At that very time, however, from Nārada, the best of sages,
the highly intelligent Mādhava, having approached him, obtained a foot-salve, / and in a few days he went to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Having bathed in the water of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, he worshiped Acyuta. / Adorned then with garlands of tulasī leaves, Mādhava,
with folded hands, spoke thus to the daughter of Jahnu, the best of rivers. / Mādhava said: “O goddess, afflicted with grief, I abandon my body in your water.
In a future birth you will give that lovely maiden to me!” / Having spoken thus and bowed down to that Gaṅgā, the mother of the three worlds,
he then began to enter the deep water. / Then Vīravara, having seized that prince from behind,
along with his men, O sage among brahmins, went swiftly toward his assembly hall. / Then, having beheld that prince, experiencing joy at his irreproachable beauty,
Vīravara spoke to him: “Who are you? Why do you abandon your body here? Speak!” / Mādhava said: “I am the son of King Vikrama, named Mādhava.
Once, for the sake of hunting, I went to a dreadful forest with my army. / In the outskirts of a city there is a lake beautified by lotuses.
There I, being lustful, saw a charming woman alone. / And she, a lovely lady named Candrakalā, seeing me overcome with love,
spoke on the earth about the matter of Sulocanā. / Then, mounted on a horse and having crossed the lord of rivers,
I went toward her city with a servant named Praceṣṭa. / On that very day her excellent pre-nuptial ceremony was taking place.
Having heard that, a letter together with a ring was sent there by me. / Having seen my letter together with the excellent ring, / what she wrote on the back of the leaf is now told:
‘There is a son of the illustrious Trivikramadeva named Vidyādhara. / My father will give me to him in marriage, O best of men.
Now the pre-nuptial rite is done; tomorrow is surely my wedding. / Even so, I shall tell a means by which you may obtain me.
Having raised my left arm, I will stand facing the groom; / whoever can carry me off, he will be my husband, without a doubt.’
Having written the letter, that maiden placed it into the hand of Gandhinī. / And by that Gandhinī, that excellent letter was given to me.
Praceṣṭa, having heard that rendezvous right before me, / mounted a horse and carried her off there, while I was overcome by sleep.
Out of that sorrow, in order to win her again back then, / listen properly, noble one, to that initial vigil according to the prescribed rules."
Having been spoken to thus, assigning many foot-soldiers for his protection, / laughing and going to the inner apartment, that maiden took on the form of a man.
Then, donning a woman's attire and adorned with various ornaments, / she sent her maidservant to bring that prince.
Coming by her order, the prince then / saw that virtuous woman like Lakṣmī incarnate.
And that maiden, rising from her golden seat, O twice-born, / bowed to his feet, her body thrilled with horripilation.
Then, according to the Gāndharva rite, that wise prince / married that maiden right there, having attained his desired delight.
Bathed in the streams of her love, the prince / spent that very night sporting with her.
Then, at pure daybreak, that virtuous, fawn-eyed woman / related the entire incident from the beginning to Mādhava.
Thereupon the virtuous Sulocanā, taking Jayantī, the king's daughter, / and Mādhava, went to Suṣeṇa's assembly.
Hearing of that maiden, the king was overjoyed and indeed / gave both Sulocanā and Jayantī to Mādhava in marriage.
As a dowry to him, that king devoted to dharma, / well pleased, gave half his kingdom and hundreds of gold pieces.
Then, having built a splendid dwelling, that prince / made his abode at that most holy sacred place, O twice-born.
Meanwhile, bringing that Praceṣṭa, who was residing in prison, / to the assembly, Mādhava thought:
"This evil-minded, cruel betrayer of his master's trust, / foremost among enemies, a fool, must not be spared by me.
Even when nurtured constantly with favors, wealth, and food, / the pitiless one merely acts as an enemy when he finds an opportunity.
The very hand that would take dust from the feet in misfortune / cuts off the master's head once prosperity is attained.
Indeed, subjects under control kill their master; / even heated water quickly brings fire to extinction."
Thinking thus in his mind, that son of the ruler of the earth, / deprived of his efforts, ceased his exertion and was repulsed, O best of the twice-born.
Then, O brahmin, that prince dwelt there happily for some time / with those two wives, free from sorrow and disease.
A hundred sons were born to high-souled Mādhava through Sulocanā, / and two hundred sons were born through Jayantī.
Mādhava's sons also became supreme knowers of weapons and treatises, / devoted to dharma for the delight of all people.
Endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu acquired in another birth, / one day that Mādhava reflected in his mind:
"Who am I? Whence have I come? Whose [creation] or by whom was I made? / Where shall I go again, or where shall I stay?
Enjoying sense objects, my life has passed without merit; / therefore, who here will rescue me, sunken in an ocean of obstacles?
Having attained human birth in this cycle of existence, he by whom Hari is not worshipped / is to be known as a slayer of his own soul, expelled from all duties.
Again and again there is birth, and again and again dissolution into the five elements; / therefore, this entire cycle of existence is distressing, terrible, and vast.
Without devotion to Viṣṇu, there can be no warding off of birth and death; / therefore, abandoning everything today, I will perform the worship of Hari."
Thinking this in his mind and sighing again and again, / he summoned Viśvakarman and spoke this word:
Mādhava said: / "O Viśvakarman of mighty arms, fashioned out of stone, make for me / an image of Viṣṇu that grants the fruit of all desires."
By his command, O brahmin, an image of Mahāviṣṇu made of stone / was then fashioned by that artisan Viśvakarman—
dark as a fresh raincloud, with eyes resembling lotuses, / holding conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and four-armed,
accompanied by Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, adorned with a forest garland, / possessing all auspicious marks, and adorned with all ornaments.
Installing that image of Hari in a splendid pavilion, / he began to worship the wielder of the discus who grants desires.
In that very temple, O brahmin, best of the twice-born, / he would offer daily a lamp of clarified butter, a lamp with an unbroken flame;
rising and bathing in the morning himself, he would sweep and do the like, / beautify the path, and smear [the floor] there again, O brahmin seer.
Having bathed in the waters where the Gaṅgā meets the ocean and performed the five great sacrifices, / he would worship Viṣṇu at the three junctures of the day with peerless offerings,
with perfumes, incense, food offerings, betel leaves, incense, and lamps, / with songs, musical instruments, compositions, and beautiful recitations of praise,
with circumambulations, prostrations, sacrifices with priestly gifts, / with meatless sacrificial food, and with diets of fruit, O virtuous one.
He would repeat the eight-syllable great mantra preceded by the Praṇava: / 'Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa,' which grants the fruit of all desires.
Thus for thousands of years, with supreme devotion, / he performed the worship granting all desires to Mahāviṣṇu, the Supreme Self.
Pleased then by his devotion, the crest-jewel of all gods, / the Lord, brilliant as a tulasī flower, appeared.
Seeing Hari manifested, Mādhava, always noble, / then embraced the earth with his head and bowed to Hari's feet.
Mādhava said: / "Obeisance to you, God of gods! Obeisance to the Supreme Self, / the Supreme Lord, Lord of the gods! Obeisance to the Giver of knowledge!
Obeisance to you, Supreme Bliss, Puruṣottama, Keśava! / Obeisance to the Lotus-eyed One, obeisance to the Lord of Kamalā!
Obeisance to you of many forms, obeisance, obeisance to the Formless One! / Obeisance to the Conceivable, the Inconceivable, the Visible, and the Invisible!
Obeisance to the Lord of the three worlds, obeisance, obeisance to the Father of the world! / Obeisance to you who are attainable through knowledge, obeisance to the Tree of all!
Obeisance to you, foe of Kaṃsa! Obeisance to the foe of Kaiṭabha! / Obeisance to you, slayer of Madhu, and obeisance, obeisance to the Ordainer!
I worship you by whom, assuming the form of a fish, / the Vedas were indeed rescued from within the waters of the deep ocean.
Obeisance, obeisance to you by whom, assuming the form of a tortoise, / this earth with its mountains and forests was borne up.
Obeisance, obeisance to you by whom, in the form of a boar, / the earth was lifted up with his own tusk, O Lord of the earth.
Obeisance, obeisance to you by whom, in the form of the Man-Lion, / the furious Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was torn apart.
Obeisance to you, O God, who in the form of a dwarf / thus destroyed the sacrifice of Bali and took [birth] from Kaśyapa.
Obeisance to you, that Rāma by whom the ancestors were propitiated / with the blood of Kṣatriyas, and by whom Kārtavīrya was slain.
Obeisance to you, that Rāma, son of Kauśalyā, / by whom Rāvaṇa, Mārīca, and Kumbhakarṇa were killed.
By whom Pralamba was slain, by you the husband of Revatī, / by the cleaver of the Kālindī—salutation to you, to that Rāma!
By whom the Vedas were reproached upon beholding the slaughter of beasts, / by you, full of compassion—salutation to you, to that Buddha!
And by whom the Mlecchas were put down at the end of the age in the form of Kalki, / for the welfare of all the worlds—salutation, salutation to you, to that one!
O Hari! O Viṣṇu! O conqueror of Daityas! O Nārāyaṇa, full of compassion! / Fallen into the terrible ocean of cyclic existence, lift me up!
Then out of joy, having washed the two feet of Hari, / having cast his whole body onto the earth, that Mādhava spoke to Hari:
Mādhava said: / O Govinda! O supreme bliss! O Mukunda! O Madhusūdana! / Protect me, a sinner, O Kṛṣṇa, since you are the destroyer of all sins!
Having heard his hymn of praise, the Lord, who is affectionate to his devotees, / attaining supreme delight, himself spoke to him these words:
The Blessed One said: / Choose a boon, O child, O Mādhava, best among kṣatriyas! / Do you desire the state of Brahmā, or the state of Śiva, or the state of Śakra, or what?
Mādhava said: / Everything has indeed been obtained by me, O Lord of the universe, there is no doubt, / since I behold you, the lord who grants boons, invisible even to the gods.
You are capable of granting everything—worldly enjoyment, liberation, wealth, and sovereignty. / O Lord, I am not worthy of devotion; grant me devotion alone!
The Blessed One said: / O child, I am pleased by this devotion of yours, there is no doubt here. / What object is there which, having given it, I may become free of debt to you?
Sūta said: / Having spoken thus, extremely pleased, extending his four arms, / Viṣṇu embraced him, O twice-born, as a father embraces a son.
The Blessed One said: / By the power of the embrace I have become free of debt to you. / All good things indeed shall happen, O blessed one; there is no doubt.
O child, my image was always worshipped with practical yoga by Kāminī; / therefore, I shall lead you to my own body.
Vyāsa said: / Having thus granted the boon to him, having again embraced [him] / with all his life-breaths with his four long arms, he disappeared right there.
Then Mādhava, along with his wife, / worshipped that image of Viṣṇu with devotion by unexcelled practical yogas.
Having enjoyed all pleasures along with his sons and grandsons, / meeting his death in the Gaṅgā, he attained liberation together with his wife.

Whoever recites with full devotion this chapter filled with the deeds of Hari, / which destroys the whole mass of sins, / having enjoyed all pleasures here in the world, in the end goes / to the abode of the blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
